Assignment 2: PCA and Clustering Analysis of a Polymerisation Reactor

CHEE4003: Special Topics A - Artificial Intelligence in Chemical Engineering

Published

August 31, 2026

Context

Modern chemical engineering systems generate large volumes of high-dimensional data from sensors, monitoring systems, and control platforms. Analysing such data is critical for understanding process behaviour, identifying operating regimes, and improving performance, safety, and efficiency.

In this assignment, a continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) is analysed. The reactor is used for the free-radical polymerisation of methyl methacrylate (MMA), with azo-bis-isobutyronitrile (AIBN) as the initiator and toluene as the solvent. This polymerisation is highly exothermic, requiring careful thermal management. A cooling jacket is therefore used to remove excess heat and regulates the system temperature.

Reactor behaviour is governed by complex interactions between multiple variables, including:

  • Temperature, which controls reaction kinetics and rate
  • Concentrations, influencing reaction progress and conversion
  • Flowrates, determining residence time and system dynamics
  • Heat generation and removal, affecting thermal stability

These coupled effects produce nonlinear system behaviour, where small changes in operating conditions can lead to significant variations in performance. As a result, the reactor operates across multiple distinct regimes, ranging from low-reactivity (e.g., startup conditions) to high-intensity reaction states, with intermediate transition regions.

Identifying and characterising these regimes is essential for effective process design and operation, enabling improved monitoring, control, and avoidance of unstable or undesirable conditions.

Engineering Challenge

Analysing this reactor system requires extracting meaningful insight from a high-dimensional dataset. In practice, engineers must address two key interconnected challenges:

1. Dimensionality Reduction: Reducing a complex dataset into a smaller set of variables while preserving the most important information about system behaviour.

2. Operating Regime Identification: Identifying groups of operating conditions that correspond to different reactor behaviours (e.g., startup, transition, steady operation).

To address these challenges, you will apply three complementary approaches to a common dataset:

  • Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) to understand data structure, patterns, and relationships
  • Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce dimensionality and identify dominant sources of variation
  • Clustering methods to detect and interpret distinct operating regimes

Assignment Aim and Learning Objectives

The aim of this assignment is to develop your ability to analyse and interpret high-dimensional chemical engineering data using data-driven techniques, and to translate these results into meaningful engineering insight.

By completing this assignment, you should be able to:

  • Analyse high-dimensional engineering datasets using appropriate statistical and visualisation techniques
  • Apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce dimensionality and identify dominant sources of variation
  • Apply clustering methods to identify and characterise natural groupings in data
  • Interpret machine learning results in terms of underlying system behaviour and engineering phenomena
  • Communicate findings clearly and effectively using well-structured visualisations and Python-based analysis

Task 1 : AI Usage Statement (6 marks)

At the beginning of your submission (details below), include a statement (maximum 0.5 page) describing your use of generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude).

Your statement should:

  • Clearly indicate whether AI tools were used
  • Describe how they were used (e.g., code generation, debugging, conceptual support)
  • Critically evaluate their usefulness and limitations in the context of your work

If you did not use generative AI tools, provide an explanation for this choice.

Task 2 : Exploratory Data Analysis (20 marks)

Using techniques introduced in Week 1, perform an exploratory data analysis (EDA) to understand the structure of the dataset, relationships between variables, and the different operating regimes of the reactor.

Your analysis should:

  • Summarise the key characteristics of the dataset (e.g., ranges, distributions, variability)
  • Explore relationships between variables using appropriate visualisations and statistics
  • Identify patterns that may indicate different operating regimes
TipTip

You are encouraged to use a combination of: summary statistics, correlation analysis, scatter plots, histograms, boxplots, and pair plots to support your analysis.

Key Questions

Address the following questions using clear evidence from your analysis:

1. Key Drivers of Reactor Behaviour
Which variable(s) appear to have the strongest influence on reactor behaviour (e.g., temperature, conversion, density)?
Support your answer with visual and statistical evidence.

2. Nature of Variable Relationships
Do the relationships between key variables appear linear or nonlinear?
Provide justification using plots and trends observed in the data.

3. Identification of Patterns
Does the dataset show evidence of distinct patterns or structure in the data?
Describe any patterns or separations observed in the data, and identify the variables that best distinguish these patterns.

ImportantImportant

Your visualisations should be purposeful and clearly interpreted. The goal is not only to present plots, but to extract meaningful insights that inform and justify your PCA and clustering analysis in subsequent tasks.

Task 3 : Principal Component Analysis - PCA (37 marks)

Using techniques introduced in Week 6, apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset and identify the dominant patterns governing reactor behaviour.

Your analysis should:

  • Prepare the dataset appropriately (e.g., standardisation of variables)
  • Apply PCA and evaluate the explained variance
  • Interpret the meaning of the principal components using the loadings
  • Relate PCA results to the underlying physical behaviour of the reactor
Tip

Use a combination of scree plots (explained variance), cumulative variance curves, loading plots, and/or PCA biplots to support your analysis. Focus on selecting an appropriate number of components, identifying the key variables driving each principal component. Link the principal components to engineering meaning (e.g., physical mechanisms, process behaviour, or system variables).

Key Questions

Address the following questions using clear evidence from your analysis:

1. Dimensionality Reduction and Explained Variance
How many principal components are required to capture most of the variance in the dataset (e.g., 80–90%)?
Evaluate whether PCA provides an effective reduction in dimensionality.

2. Interpretation of Principal Components
What physical meaning can be assigned to the main principal components?
- PC1: Which variables contribute most strongly to PC1? What type of behaviour or variation might this component represent?
- PC2: Which variables contribute most strongly to PC2? How does this component differ from PC1 in the type of variation it captures?
Support your answer using loadings and variable contributions.

3. Engineering Interpretation
How do the principal components relate to the underlying behaviour of the reactor system?
Discuss how the principal components help explain the factors that drive variation in the system

Task 4 : Clustering Analysis (37 marks)

Using techniques introduced in Week 7, apply clustering methods to the PCA-transformed dataset, using only the first two principal components (PC1 and PC2), to identify distinct operating regimes in the reactor data.

The following clustering methods should be used:

  • K-Means Clustering Algorithm
  • Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN)
  • Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM)

Your analysis should:

  • Apply each clustering method to the reduced-dimensional dataset
  • Clearly justify the choice of parameters (e.g., number of clusters, epsilon, minimum samples)
  • Visualise the clustering results, for example using PCA score plots coloured by cluster labels
  • Interpret the identified clusters in terms of reactor behaviour
TipTip

Use appropriate metrics to guide parameter selection, such as silhouette score and inertia (for K-Means), and AIC or BIC (for GMM). For DBSCAN, silhouette score can be used (computed on non-noise points), but should be interpreted with caution due irregular cluster shapes.

Key Questions

Address the following questions using clear evidence from your analysis:

1. Cluster Identification and Structure
For each clustering method:
- How many clusters are identified?
- How are the clusters distributed in the PCA space?
- Do the clusters show clear separation or overlap?
- For DBSCAN, are there any points are classified as noise, and how are these distributed?

2. Comparison of Clustering Methods
Compare the performance of K-Means, GMM, and DBSCAN:
- How do the clustering structures differ between methods?
- Which method produces the most interpretable grouping?
- Which method captures more complex or subtle patterns?

3. Identification of Operating Regimes
Using the results from one selected clustering method, answer the following:
- Do the clusters correspond to distinct operating regimes (e.g., low conversion, high reaction rate, transition states)?
- Which variables appear to distinguish these regimes?
Support your answer using visual evidence (e.g., PCA plots coloured by cluster labels) and appropriate interpretation.

4. Engineering Interpretation
Interpret the clusters in terms of reactor operation:
- What types of operating conditions do the clusters represent?
- How do clusters differ in terms of process behaviour?
- What insights do these groupings provide about reactor performance?
- For DBSCAN, comment on the physical significance of noise points (if any) and whether they indicate outliers, transitions between regimes, or unstable operating conditions

ImportantImportant

You must compare all three clustering methods using the same PCA-reduced dataset. Focus on justified parameter selection, not exhaustive grid searches. Emphasis is on interpretation and insight, not just applying algorithms. Clearly link clustering results to physical reactor behaviour.

Submission

Submit your work via Gradescope. Your submission must include:

1. Report

Submit a single, well-structured report of 6–9 pages (use the space effectively). The report should be clear, concise, and professionally presented, and must include:

  • Relevant figures, tables, and results
  • Complete written responses to all questions
  • Interpretation of results and justification of conclusions
TipTip

Use a small number of high-quality, informative figures and tables. Avoid repetitive or unnecessary figures.

ImportantReport Requirements
  • Ensure all figures and tables are clearly labelled and referenced in the text
  • Present results succinctly, emphasising interpretation and insight rather than raw outputs
  • Marks are awarded for both technical accuracy and engineering insight

2. Code

Submit a single Python file called a2.py. The code must be:

  • Well-organised and easy to read
  • Written using meaningful variable and function names
  • Properly commented to explain key steps
ImportantCode Requirements

The submitted code script must:

  • Execute successfully in the Gradescope autograder environment.
  • Generate and reproduce all figures, analyses, and results presented in the report.
  • Be tested in Gradescope before submission.

Students are responsible for ensuring that their code runs correctly and produces reproducible results in the Gradescope assessment environment.

Failure to submit your code script or submission of code that does not execute successfully and reproduce the reported results, will result in a penalty of 50% of the total assignment mark. This penalty will be applied regardless of the quality of the accompanying report.

Marking Rubric

Marks are awarded based on the quality of analysis, interpretation, justification, and engineering insight. Higher marks require conclusions to be supported by appropriate evidence and clearly communicated.
